## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.

  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag

  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.

WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.

  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: All five Section B matches are tagged 'unclassified' with category 'file_ops' — none carries a specific attack tag (no credential-harvesting, exfiltration, backdoor, C2, or typosquatting). Section A shows only its documented media-pipeline behavior: creating a temp file via tempfile.mkstemp with a suffix derived from a string literal (file extension), plus ordinary string/path manipulation and Pillow's DecompressionBombError image-validation guard. There is no undocumented outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or decoded-payload execution. Section B's high similarity scores come entirely from unclassified file_ops neighbors and low-confidence generic GuardDog YARA heuristics, which per RULE 2 represent shape overlap rather than confirmed malicious intent. Verdict: BENIGN.

## Source: amazon-inspector (5a6449a8f35de848928e7f17d88c87db80e5aee40e8b53c375e07fc7d43cc05e)
On every `import disksweep`, the package's top-level `src/disksweep/__init__.py` (lines 18-24) calls `ctypes.CDLL` on a 2.9 MB Windows binary (`_parser.pyd`) shipped inside the wheel. Loading a Windows PE via `ctypes.CDLL` invokes the DLL's `DllMain(DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH)` entry point, executing whatever native code the binary contains in the importing process. No Python code in the package ever calls into the DLL — it is loaded purely for its load-time side effects, and any exception is silently swallowed (`except: pass`). The README explicitly advertises 'Zero dependencies. Nothing to audit.' and the pure-Python `scan.py` already implements the full scanner functionality, so the binary's presence is unjustified by the advertised feature set. `pyproject.toml` (lines 87, 90) additionally force-includes a byte-identical copy of the binary under a second name (`__parser.pyd`, sha256 b1aace6c…f83c3, 2,905,600 bytes) that has no Python reference — a redundancy pattern consistent with AV-evasion / fallback-loading rather than a legitimate native acceleration library. Any Windows host that runs `pip install disksweep` followed by `import disksweep`, or invokes the `disksweep`/`sweep` CLI (which imports the package), will execute the opaque native code.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

No install-time hooks, no undocumented outbound destinations, no credential reads outside the package's own request configuration, no decoded-payload execution.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Top Section B match is 0.80 (httpie-edgegrid, unclassified) and the remaining matches are also unclassified/untagged or generic research-campaign entries. Per RULE 2, similarity built on generic shapes (base64 encoding, network calls, error handling) with unclassified neighbors is shape overlap, not evidence of intent. No match carries a specific confirmed attack tag at >=0.85, so Section B does not override the clean Q1 finding.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: The base64 usage is standard HTTP Basic authentication header construction (base64.b64encode of credentials prefixed with 'Basic '), a documented, expected feature of an HTTP client/scraping library. malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Overlap on base64 encoding of credentials and HTTP auth header construction, plus generic network/error-handling call shapes. The matched neighbor is unclassified, so the overlap reflects common legitimate auth/HTTP code shape rather than shared malicious intent.

This is fully explained by the package's documented HTTP client functionality, with no install-time side effects, undocumented destinations, or credential access beyond the caller-supplied request config. Section B's 0.80 similarity is to an unclassified package and reflects generic base64/network code shape, not confirmed malicious intent. Verdict: BENIGN.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

reasoning.code_intent: Section A describes base64 encode/decode operations (b64encode/b64decode, base64Pattern.match) and SASL authentication error handling (SASLIncorrectEncodingError, SASLNoAcceptableMechanism, mechanisms.append) plus XML parsing (failure.firstChildElement). The 'auth.addContent(b64encode(data).decode("ascii") or "=")' pattern is the standard SASL/XML auth payload construction used in Scrapy's HTTP authentication handling — encoding credentials into a base64 auth blob for a request. The data sources are string literals (mechanism names, encoding constants), and the sinks are internal auth content nodes. No outbound call to an undocumented destination, no credential read outside the auth flow, no install-time hook, no decoded-payload execution.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Top match is genesisbot at 0.91, tagged 'unclassified' — an untagged neighbor, so per RULE 2 the similarity reflects generic code shape (base64 + auth/encoding handling) rather than confirmed malicious intent. The metadata-checker matches (0.90) carry specific tags (data_exfiltration, spyware_infostealer), but those samples are described as exfiltrating hardcoded data to an obfuscated destination — a pattern absent from Section A, which shows no exfiltration destination. The dbnodeindicator match (0.89) is a supply-chain downloader, also absent here. Since Q1 found no independent anomaly, the high scores do not override the clean finding.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: The base64 encode/decode and SASL auth handling is Scrapy's own documented HTTP authentication mechanism construction — encoding credentials into an auth header/content node. This is standard, legitimate protocol handling with no exfiltration destination, no credential access outside the auth flow, and no install-time side effect.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Overlap on base64 encoding/decoding primitives and auth/encoding string handling, which are generic shapes shared by legitimate protocol libraries and malware alike; the matched neighbor is unclassified, so the overlap does not indicate shared intent.

mitre_mapping.relevance: Base64 decode operations present, but used for standard auth payload handling, not obfuscation of malicious content.

llm_evaluation.summary: Section A shows Scrapy's standard SASL/HTTP authentication handling: base64 encoding of auth data into an XML content node, SASL mechanism negotiation, and XML parsing of failure elements. Every action is fully explained by the package's documented HTTP auth functionality — there is no undocumented outbound destination, no credential access outside the auth flow, and no install-time side effect. Section B's top match (genesisbot, 0.91) is unclassified, so the similarity reflects generic base64/auth code shape rather than confirmed malicious intent; the tagged metadata-checker matches describe exfiltration behavior that is absent from this code. Verdict: BENIGN.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

reasoning.code_intent: Section A describes a dynamic import of a Python stdlib encoding module via importlib.import_module(f"encodings.{iana_name}") and instantiation of its IncrementalDecoder. This is the standard mechanism used by HTTP libraries (including Scrapy's charset handling and its dependency charset-normalizer) to resolve an IANA-declared charset name to a Python codec for decoding response bodies. The data source is a string literal (the IANA charset name), the sink is an f-string used to build the module path, and the surrounding calls (FREQUENCIES.items, .lower, .join, abs, any, bytes, OSError/ValueError handling) are consistent with charset detection/decoding logic. There is no outbound network call, no credential access, no install-time hook, no file write outside normal cache/config paths, and no execution of decoded content. Every observed action is fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented charset-decoding functionality.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B's top match (open-vp-cal, 0.86) carries specific tags (credential_stealer, data_exfiltration, spyware_infostealer, supply_chain_downloader), but Q1 found no independent anomaly in this package's behavior. Per RULE 2, the similarity reflects generic code-shape overlap (dynamic import + string formatting + encoding handling), not shared intent. The matched neighbor's malicious behavior (remote package installation, credential theft) is not present in Section A. A high score alone does not override a clean, specifically-explained Q1 finding.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: The dynamic import of encodings.{iana_name} and IncrementalDecoder usage is the standard, documented mechanism for resolving IANA charset names to Python codecs during HTTP response decoding — a core part of Scrapy's and charset-normalizer's legitimate functionality. No anomalous data flow, network call, or install-time side effect is present.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Structural overlap in dynamic import chains (importlib.import_module with f-string module paths) and encoding/decoding logic. The matched sample uses similar shapes for malicious remote package installation and credential theft, but this package's use is confined to legitimate charset resolution.

mitre_mapping.relevance: Dynamic import via importlib.import_module can be used for obfuscation, but here it is a documented charset-resolution pattern, not obfuscation.

llm_evaluation.summary: Section A shows Scrapy performing standard IANA charset resolution via importlib.import_module(f"encodings.{iana_name}") and IncrementalDecoder — a documented, legitimate mechanism for decoding HTTP response bodies. No outbound calls, credential access, install-time side effects, or execution of decoded payloads are present. Section B's 0.86 similarity to open-vp-cal reflects generic code-shape overlap (dynamic imports, encoding logic) rather than shared malicious intent; the matched sample's specific attack tags are not corroborated by any independent anomaly in this package. Verdict: BENIGN, false positive.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

The data flow is StringLiteral -> List (fromlist) -> package (module name) -> __import__ -> getattr, which is exactly the plugin/loader idiom. There is no network call, no credential access, no install-time hook, no decoded payload, and no write outside documented config/cache paths.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Top Section B match is keras-arg at 0.86, tagged 'unclassified' with no analyst description; the remaining matches (Nasrtox, managment, ehtereum, node-db-indicator) are also unclassified or carry only generic process_exec/supply_chain tags with no specific attack tag tied to this dynamic-import shape. reasoning.false_positive_reason: The dynamic import chain (__import__ with fromlist, getattr, ImportError handling, name.rsplit) is Scrapy's own documented object-loading utility used to resolve dotted paths for spiders, middlewares, pipelines, and extensions. No independently anomalous behavior is present.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Structural overlap on the generic dynamic-import idiom (string module name -> __import__ -> getattr). The matched sample is unclassified with no analyst description, so the similarity reflects a common legitimate plugin-loading shape rather than a confirmed malicious pattern.

llm_evaluation.summary: Section A shows only Scrapy's standard dynamic object-loading helper: a dotted module string is passed to __import__ with a fromlist and the target attribute is retrieved via getattr, with ImportError handling and name.rsplit for path parsing. This is fully explained by Scrapy's documented plugin/spider/middleware loading functionality, with no network egress, credential access, install-time side effect, or decoded-payload execution. Section B's top match (keras-arg, 0.86) is unclassified and untagged, and all other matches are likewise unclassified or carry only generic process_exec tags, so the similarity reduces to generic code-shape overlap per RULE 2 and does not override the clean Q1 finding. Verdict: BENIGN.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.

WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.

    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for

  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.

reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

**RULE 1 — PACKAGE NAME ≠ PACKAGE IDENTITY:**
You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

**RULE 2 — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT INTENT, UNLESS A MATCH IS TAG-CONFIRMED:**
base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing
crypto, a logger writing log files, or a serialization library using dynamic
imports for its own documented plugin system are not.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
## ANALYSIS

**Q1 — What does the code do, and is anything about it unexplained?**
Describe ONLY what Section A shows (not what the package name implies):
data sources, data destinations, install-time hooks, network calls,
credential access, obfuscation patterns.
Then answer directly: is there a SPECIFIC action here that is NOT fully
accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if
so (e.g., "writes to a path outside any documented config/cache location",
"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

**Q2 — Does Section B change this assessment?**
State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.
- If Q1 found NO independent anomaly: Section B's score, however high, is
  evidence of generic shape overlap (RULE 2), not of intent. It does not
  override a clean Q1 finding. Say so explicitly rather than defaulting to
  suspicion because the number is high.
- If Q1 DID find a specific anomaly: does Section B corroborate it? Check
  EVERY match listed in Section B, not only the highest-ranked one — a
  SPECIFIC, non-generic attack tag (e.g., "credential-harvesting",
  "data-exfiltration", "backdoor", "C2", "typosquatting") on ANY match at
  meaningfully high similarity (≥ 0.85) IS corroboration, regardless of
  whether it happens to be ranked #1 or lower among the matches shown. A
  specific tag means a human analyst already confirmed that exact pattern
  in a different sample — this counts as corroboration EVEN WHEN the
  underlying code pattern (dynamic import, encoding, process execution) is
  itself common. RULE 2's caution about "generic shapes" applies to
  matches that are THEMSELVES unclassified/untagged — where you cannot
  tell whether the shape correlates with confirmed intent — not to matches
  that already carry a specific attack tag. Do not use RULE 2 to discount
  a specific tag just because the shape is common; that is what the tag
  is for. Only if EVERY match in Section B is unclassified/untagged does
  the similarity reduce to generic-shape overlap, in which case Q1's own
  finding stands on its own merits.

**Q3 — Final verdict.**
Choose: MALICIOUS | BENIGN. This is a BINARY decision — there is no
"monitor for now, not sure yet" middle option. Every case must resolve to
one or the other.
- BENIGN: Q1 found no independently anomalous behavior — every action is
  fully and specifically explained by ordinary, documented functionality.
  This holds REGARDLESS of the Section B similarity score — a clean,
  specifically-explained Q1 finding is not overridden by a high similarity
  number alone.
- MALICIOUS: everything else. Q1 found something not FULLY and
  SPECIFICALLY explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — this
  includes cases where Q1 itself is uncertain ("could be legitimate X, but
  could also be Y") as well as cases where Q1 is fully confident nothing
  legitimate accounts for it, and regardless of whether Section B
  corroborates with a specific tag or not. Do NOT hedge into a soft middle
  verdict: if you cannot fully and specifically explain the behavior via
  BENIGN's criteria above, the verdict is MALICIOUS. A specific attack tag
  in Section B (per Q2) or an unambiguous anomaly on its own both justify a
  HIGHER ssvc_decision (ATTEND/ACT rather than TRACK*, see below) but are
  not required to reach the MALICIOUS verdict itself once Q1 has identified
  something genuinely unexplained.
SSVC_DECISION GRANULARITY: use ssvc_decision to express your confidence
WITHIN the binary verdict, for downstream triage — it does not change the
verdict itself.
  - verdict BENIGN → ssvc_decision TRACK.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, but Q1's anomaly is genuinely tentative and Section B
    gives no specific-tag corroboration → ssvc_decision TRACK* (flag for
    human review, lower confidence).
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with either a specific-tag corroboration (Q2) or a
    clearly-identified anomaly → ssvc_decision ATTEND.
  - verdict MALICIOUS, with an unambiguous, confirmed malicious pattern
    (confirmed credential exfiltration, confirmed C2, confirmed execution
    of an undocumented decoded payload) → ssvc_decision ACT.
CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT: is_false_positive in your JSON output must directly
reflect your Q1 finding and must agree with verdict: true only when verdict
is BENIGN, false whenever verdict is MALICIOUS. Do not let these fields
disagree with each other or with Q1.

## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious
— this is real evidence, and it is NOT cancelled out by the fact that the
underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,
not contradictory ones — do not use the former to dismiss the latter. Judge
by what the data flows TO: an outbound call to an undocumented destination,
a credential read with no connection to the package's stated purpose, or an
install-time side effect are real signals. A crypto library performing

accounted for by ordinary, documented functionality? Name it precisely if

"makes an outbound call to a destination with no connection to the
package's stated purpose", "decodes and executes content whose purpose is
never referenced elsewhere in the visible code"). If every action has a
clear, specific, legitimate explanation, say so explicitly: "no
independently anomalous behavior — [state the specific legitimate
explanation, e.g. 'this is the package's own documented crypto IV handling'
or 'standard logging file-path setup']."

State the top similarity score and the matched neighbor's tag.

No anomalous outbound calls, credential access, install-time side effects, or decoded payload execution are present. Although Section B shows high structural similarity (0.93) to unclassified/process-exec and spyware-tagged samples, this reflects generic code-shape overlap rather than malicious intent, and Q1 provides a specific legitimate explanation. Verdict: BENIGN.
